title: IS MARITAL SEX ONLY FOR MAKING BABIES? Proverbs and Song of Songs Complicate That Answer
paragraphs: IS MARITAL SEX ONLY FOR MAKING BABIES? Proverbs and Song of Songs Complicate That Answer
If you were taught that a husband and wife should only come together to produce children, there are passages in your Bible that may make you uncomfortable—and perhaps they are supposed to.
There are subjects Christians can discuss over coffee without lowering their voices.
Grace.
Prayer.
Faith.
Heaven.
Marriage.
Then someone says the word “sex,” and suddenly the room changes.
Eyes move.
People become careful.
Some become embarrassed.
Some become defensive.
And some quietly carry wounds nobody in the room knows exist.
Because for many Christians, sexuality was never actually discipled.
It was merely warned about.
“Don’t.”
“Wait.”
“Stay pure.”
“Flee temptation.”
Those warnings matter. Scripture takes sexual holiness seriously.
But then a Christian gets married.
And sometimes the message they have absorbed for years does not magically disappear at the altar.
The person who spent years hearing that sexual desire was dangerous may now be expected to believe that marital desire is beautiful.
The person who learned to associate the body with shame may suddenly be told to receive the body of a spouse as a gift.
And somewhere beneath all of this sits a question Christians have wrestled with for centuries:
Is sex within marriage ultimately only for having children?
Children are unquestionably one of God's great gifts.
The Bible opens with God's blessing over humanity:
“Be fruitful, and multiply” (Genesis 1:28, KJV).
The Hebrew behind “be fruitful” is פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ — peru urevu — “be fruitful and multiply.”
Human fertility is not treated as an embarrassment in Scripture.
Children are not accidents interrupting the “real” purpose of marriage. Psalm 127 calls children a heritage from the LORD.

So any Christian understanding of marriage that despises fertility, treats children as inherently undesirable, or disconnects sexuality completely from the life-giving design of our bodies has missed something important.
But something else is equally important.
Genesis does not stop at reproduction.
Before sin enters the world, before shame enters the human experience, before broken desire and exploitation appear, Genesis says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vehayu levasar echad.
“They shall become one flesh.”
Not merely producers of offspring.
One flesh.
A covenant union involving the whole person.
Then you turn several hundred pages.
And Proverbs says something startling.
Not because it is vulgar.
Because it is holy.
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Scripture becomes even more direct:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:18–19.
Read it again.
Slowly.
God did not accidentally leave those words in the Bible.
The Hebrew is striking.
The final thought includes:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The imagery carries the sense of continually being captivated, exhilarated, even intoxicated by her love.
The passage is not instructing a husband merely to tolerate intimacy long enough to produce an heir.
It tells him to rejoice in his wife.
To delight in her.
To remain captivated by her love.
And notice the context.
Proverbs 5 is a warning against adultery.
The answer to forbidden sexuality is not the destruction of sexuality.
It is covenant faithfulness.
Scripture does not say, “Stop desiring.”
It redirects desire home.
There is something profoundly beautiful about that.
God's answer to lust is not lovelessness.
His answer to adultery is not marital coldness.
His answer to counterfeit intimacy includes the recovery of covenant intimacy.
And then you reach the Song of Songs.
If Proverbs makes some Christians uncomfortable, Song of Songs can make them wonder how the book ever survived a church committee.
It is poetry.
It is sophisticated.
Its imagery requires interpretation with humility.
Christians throughout history have also seen theological symbolism in its love poetry.
But whatever additional theological applications one recognizes, the text itself unmistakably celebrates the longing, beauty, exclusivity, and delight of human love.
The lovers notice one another.
They miss one another.
They praise one another's bodies.
They desire closeness.
They speak with an intensity that would sound almost scandalous if people had forgotten that God created marriage.
The bride says:
“Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits.”
Song of Songs 4:16.
And here is what cannot honestly be ignored:
The immediate poetic scene is not discussing conception.
There is no command in that verse to produce a child.
There is delight.
Invitation.
Mutual desire.
Belonging.
Love.
That does not erase the procreative dimension of marital sexuality.
It proves something more nuanced.
The Bible is capable of celebrating marital intimacy without making procreation the explicit subject of every embrace.
That matters.
Because some couples are infertile.
Some are elderly.
Some desperately want children and cannot conceive.
Some have endured miscarriage.
Some carry medical limitations.
Some have experienced sexual trauma.
Some marriages have spent years trying to recover tenderness after betrayal, pornography, resentment, exhaustion, childbirth, illness, grief, or emotional distance.
Imagine telling an infertile husband and wife that their sexual union has somehow lost its meaning because conception is impossible.
Scripture does not speak that way.
Imagine Abraham and Sarah in old age.
Imagine an elderly covenant couple whose childbearing years are gone.
Does tenderness suddenly become pointless?
Does affection expire when fertility does?
Proverbs answers with language that refuses to reduce marital love to reproduction:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
There is something breathtaking hidden in those words.
She is the wife of your youth.
But Proverbs is envisioning a love that continues.
Bodies change.
Faces change.
Hair changes.
Strength changes.
Pregnancy may come.
Infertility may come.
Children may fill the house.
Eventually children may leave it.
And two people who once stood trembling before an altar may one day look across a quiet room at faces marked by decades.
Still yours.
Still mine.
Still covenant.
Still beloved.
That is far more beautiful than a theology that treats a spouse like reproductive machinery.
And then Paul walks into the conversation.
First Corinthians 7:3–5 is sometimes quoted badly, especially when someone wants to demand sex from a spouse.
But read Paul's actual symmetry.
The husband has obligations toward the wife.
The wife has obligations toward the husband.
Then Paul makes a remarkably reciprocal statement concerning authority over their bodies.
And when he speaks of temporary abstinence, he uses the Greek expression:
ἐκ συμφώνου
ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
By mutual consent.
The word is related to the idea of being in harmony—“sounding together.”
Paul does not describe unilateral domination.
He describes reciprocity.
Then he tells married believers who temporarily abstain for prayer to come together again.
Think about the implication.
Paul does not say:
“Resume relations only when you intend to conceive.”
He recognizes sexual union as an ongoing dimension of marriage.
That does not mean a spouse can weaponize 1 Corinthians 7.
Never.
Biblical mutuality cannot legitimately be turned into permission for coercion, intimidation, manipulation, marital rape, or abuse.
A body entrusted in covenant is not a body available for cruelty.
Christian marriage should make a person safer, not more afraid.
The same Christ who calls husbands and wives into profound union calls His people to sacrificial love.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” (Ephesians 5:25).
Look at Jesus.
His model of authority is self-giving.
Not exploitation.
Not selfish appetite.
Not “You owe me.”
The cross destroys that kind of entitlement.
Christ gives Himself.
And suddenly the question becomes deeper than:
“What am I allowed to do?”
Christian marriage asks:
“How can I love this person entrusted to me in a way that reflects Christ?”
That changes everything.
Sex becomes neither god nor garbage.
Neither an idol to worship nor dirt to despise.
It becomes something that belongs beneath the lordship of Jesus.
And perhaps this is where some of us need healing.
Because you may have entered this article expecting a theological argument.
Instead, something personal surfaced.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.
Maybe you sleep inches apart physically and miles apart emotionally.
Maybe pornography taught you to consume bodies instead of cherish a person.
Maybe betrayal shattered something you thought would never break.
Maybe you have been rejected so many times that you stopped reaching.
Maybe you were pressured so often that tenderness now feels dangerous.
Maybe infertility made every intimate moment feel like a medical appointment.
Maybe years of trying to conceive turned something once tender into calendars, tests, disappointment, and tears behind a locked bathroom door.
Maybe someone used Scripture against you.
Maybe nobody ever told you that God cares about what happened to you.
And perhaps you need to hear this:
Jesus Christ did not come merely to regulate behavior.
He came to redeem people.
Shame says, “Hide.”
Jesus keeps calling people into the light.
Sin says, “Use.”
Jesus teaches us to love.
Lust says, “Take.”
Christ says, “Give yourself.”
Adultery says, “Break covenant for desire.”
Jesus can teach wounded people how to bring desire back beneath covenant.
Pornography says, “This body exists for your consumption.”
The Gospel says the person before you bears the image of God.
And grace says something scandalous to every sinner who has failed sexually:
Your sin can be forgiven.
Not excused.
Forgiven.
There is a difference.
The Gospel does not rename darkness as light.
It brings sinners out of darkness.
At the cross, Jesus carried real guilt.
Real sexual sin.
Real adultery.
Real lust.
Real pornography.
Real secret histories.
Real impurity.
Real selfishness.
Real shame.
And when a sinner comes to Christ in repentance and faith, grace does not merely cover the scandal like someone throwing a sheet over a crime scene.
Christ begins rewriting the person.
That is why our message has never been that scandal does not matter.
Our message is that scandal does not get the final word when Jesus enters the story.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you crossed lines before marriage.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe you became addicted to pornography.
Maybe your imagination became a place you would be terrified for anyone else to see.
Repent.
But do not confuse repentance with despair.
The blood of Jesus is stronger than the chapter you are ashamed to reread.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Cleanse.
Not merely tolerate.
Cleanse.
This is Christianity.
Not pretending the stain was never there.
Being washed by Christ.
And perhaps the church needs to recover the courage to say two truths at the same time:
Sexual immorality is serious.
And marital sexuality is not dirty.
Pornography is not Song of Songs.
Adultery is not Proverbs 5.
Lust is not covenant delight.
Coercion is not 1 Corinthians 7.
God's boundaries do not exist because sex is evil.
Boundaries protect something powerful enough to wound people deeply when severed from faithfulness, truth, covenant, and love.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the house destroys it.
The answer is not to hate fire.
The answer is to honor where it belongs.
So...
Is marital sex only for making babies?
The whole biblical witness makes that reduction difficult to sustain.
Procreation is profoundly important in Scripture.
“One flesh” union is also important.
Faithfulness is important.
Mutual care is important.
Marital delight is important.
Tenderness is important.
And Scripture itself can celebrate a husband delighting in his wife and lovers longing for one another without mentioning conception in every scene.
Proverbs does not blush.
Song of Songs does not apologize.
Paul does not describe marriage as a reproductive transaction.
And Jesus brings every dimension of our lives—including sexuality—under His redeeming lordship.
Maybe what needs to be rescued is not sexual license.
Maybe what needs rescuing is holy intimacy itself.
Rescued from pornography.
Rescued from selfishness.
Rescued from coercion.
Rescued from shame.
Rescued from adultery.
Rescued from performance.
Rescued from the idea that a spouse is either a temptation to fear or an object to use.
Back to covenant.
Back to tenderness.
Back to truth.
Back to Christ.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't pretend it didn't.
No details required.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another believer, “Please stand with me.”
And yes, even send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
One share can place biblical truth in front of someone we may never have been able to reach ourselves.
It cannot.
It does not.
Scripture tells believers to give willingly rather than under compulsion.
Your support helps keep the mission moving.
And there is another way you can help without spending anything:
Share.
A Facebook share costs you nothing, but it can carry the Gospel farther than you know.
Pray.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help where wounds are deep.
Love your spouse as a person, not an object.
Bring hidden sin into the light.
Bring wounded intimacy before Jesus.
And never forget that Christianity is not the story of clean people avoiding dirty people.
It is the story of a holy Savior rescuing sinners.
Maybe even you.
Maybe especially the part of you nobody sees.
Because the most scandalous thing in your story may not be what you did, what was done to you, or what nearly destroyed your marriage.
The most unforgettable part may be discovering that Jesus was willing to enter the chapter you wanted to tear out—and begin writing redemption there.
